weeks.title: Cost & Variance Analysis — From Job Cost to GL (CMA P1-C · feeds FAR/AUD)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — a $390,000.00 variance with a real cause

Real MBG finding: Brookhaven account 405 totaled $6,140,000.00 and was correct; no journal entry was needed. Yet job-cost-to-GL comparison showed a $390,000.00 variance caused by prior-year costs posted to the GL that bypassed the Job Cost module. The CTL batch number was the cross-account link used to trace coding.

This is why a variance is a question, not an entry. Posting $390,000.00 merely to force two totals to agree would have destroyed the valid GL and concealed the incomplete subsidiary history. Performance management requires decomposing differences into volume, price, efficiency, mix, cutoff, classification, and system-path causes.

Concept — standards and variance layers

A standard cost represents expected input quantity and price for a defined level and method of output. Standards support planning, control, inventory costing where applicable, and performance evaluation. Ideal standards assume perfect conditions; currently attainable standards allow normal downtime, waste, and inefficiency. Standards must be updated when process or market conditions change, but not merely to erase unfavorable results.

Variance analysis compares actual results with a valid benchmark. Start by selecting the correct comparison:

  • Actual versus static budget combines activity and performance effects.
  • Actual versus flexible budget isolates spending and efficiency at actual activity.
  • Flexible versus static budget shows activity-volume effect.
  • Actual versus current forecast measures forecast accuracy, not necessarily controllable performance.
  • Job-cost subsidiary versus GL tests system completeness and classification, not operating efficiency.

Direct-material variances

For materials:

Price variance = Actual quantity purchased × (Actual price − Standard price)

Quantity variance = Standard price × (Actual quantity used − Standard quantity allowed)

Assume illustratively that 11,000 units were purchased and used at $5.20, while standard is 10,000 units at $5.00 for actual output. Price variance is 11,000 × ($5.20 − $5.00) = $2,200 unfavorable. Quantity variance is $5.00 × (11,000 − 10,000) = $5,000 unfavorable. Total material cost variance is $7,200 unfavorable, tying actual $57,200 to standard allowed $50,000.

Responsibility may differ: procurement influences price, while operations influence usage, but quality, rush orders, supplier failures, design changes, and purchasing lot size can cross boundaries. Variance labels do not prove responsibility.

Direct-labor and variable-overhead variances

For labor:

Rate variance = Actual hours × (Actual rate − Standard rate)

Efficiency variance = Standard rate × (Actual hours − Standard hours allowed)

Assume illustratively 1,050 hours at $31 versus 1,000 standard hours at $30. Rate variance is 1,050 × $1 = $1,050 unfavorable. Efficiency variance is $30 × 50 = $1,500 unfavorable. Total is $2,550 unfavorable; actual $32,550 minus standard $30,000 ties.

Variable-overhead spending and efficiency variances use the actual and standard variable-overhead rate with the allocation base. Efficiency reflects base usage, not necessarily overhead department performance. Fixed-overhead spending compares actual fixed overhead with budget; production-volume variance measures the effect of actual output differing from denominator activity used to apply fixed overhead.

Flexible-budget worked example

Assume an illustrative job budget of $200 variable cost per installed unit plus $40,000 fixed support. Planned activity is 500 units, so static budget is $140,000. Actual activity is 550 units; flexible budget is $150,000. Actual cost is $158,000.

LayerCalculationVariance
Activity$150,000 flexible − $140,000 static$10,000 due to higher activity
Spending/efficiency$158,000 actual − $150,000 flexible$8,000 unfavorable
Total vs static$158,000 − $140,000$18,000 unfavorable

Only $8,000 is unfavorable after allowing for actual activity. Calling the entire $18,000 “overspending” would misdiagnose the result.

Reconcile systems before judging operations

The real Brookhaven $390,000.00 difference was not a price or efficiency variance. It was a population difference: valid prior-year GL costs bypassed job cost. Use this sequence:

  1. Fix entity, exact account, job, and period.
  2. Compute true JCS ending balances; do not trust the last row.
  3. Reconcile GL and job-cost populations by CTL/batch and transaction.
  4. Classify differences as timing, bypass, miscode, duplication, or unsupported.
  5. Correct only when evidence shows a ledger error.
  6. Then compare valid actuals with budget, standard, and forecast.

A suppressed zero-balance job-cost account can create a false TB variance. Exact account matching avoids substring contamination. A rollforward of totals is insufficient; unexplained variance must be $0.00.

Investigation and management action

Set investigation thresholds using amount, percentage, recurrence, trend, risk, and controllability. A large favorable material-price variance may reflect low quality and later unfavorable usage. A favorable labor-efficiency variance can coincide with schedule delay if output measurement is incomplete.

Use a variance bridge with baseline, volume, price/rate, quantity/efficiency, mix, yield, scope, cutoff, and classification. Assign action to the cause: renegotiate supplier terms, update standards, improve training, correct mapping, accrue missing cost, or change forecast. Avoid punishing managers for external or upstream causes they could not influence; otherwise they will game data.

Close the loop by measuring whether the action worked. Repeated explanations without action convert variance reporting into ritual. Preserve original standards and approval for revisions so improvement is not manufactured by rebasing.

Mix, yield, and overhead detail

When multiple inputs create output, split quantity variance into mix and yield. A mix variance measures the cost effect of using input proportions different from standard. A yield variance measures whether total input produced the expected output. In construction, substituting a cheaper material may create favorable mix but unfavorable yield through waste or rework. Define equivalent output carefully before applying manufacturing formulas to unique jobs.

Sales and contribution variances can also be decomposed into market size, market share, selling price, sales volume, and mix when reliable market data exists. Do not attribute market movement to a manager as though it were controllable volume. Use contribution margin rather than revenue alone when product or job mix differs.

Fixed-overhead production-volume variance is driven by denominator activity used to establish the rate. It is not the same as a cash overspend. Underutilized capacity can create unfavorable volume variance even when actual fixed cost equals budget. Spending variance compares actual fixed overhead with its budget. Keep capacity economics visible rather than allocating every idle-cost dollar to active jobs.

For each variance, document formula, source, sign convention, threshold, explanation, owner, and action. A favorable/unfavorable label depends on account type and objective. Higher revenue is generally favorable; higher cost generally unfavorable; higher preventive-maintenance cost may be favorable strategically if it avoids downtime. Narrative should explain business effect, not merely repeat the sign.

Validate mathematical closure. Total material variance must equal actual material cost minus standard cost allowed, and components must sum to the total under the chosen timing convention. If they do not, quantity bases, purchase/use timing, or standards are inconsistent. A variance report that fails its own bridge is not ready for management.

CPA Crossover — FAR and AUD

FAR asks whether job-cost and GL balances support asset and expense reporting. AUD asks whether interfaces, cutoff, and reconciliations are reliable. A management variance may become an audit indicator, but it is not audit evidence until the underlying population and logic are validated.

Practice and recap

  1. Reconcile actual data before calculating performance variance.
  2. Select static, flexible, standard, forecast, or ledger comparison deliberately.
  3. Decompose total differences using consistent formulas.
  4. Trace cause across procurement, operations, finance, and systems.
  5. Correct the wrong record—not the number that is harder to explain.
  6. Track actions and standard changes.

Recap: Brookhaven teaches the central rule: a real variance can reflect system path rather than bad performance. Reconcile the population, preserve the valid $6,140,000.00 balance, and use the $390,000.00 difference to diagnose missing job-cost history.

weeks.title: Responsibility Centers & Transfer Pricing (CMA P1-C · feeds BAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — reciprocal accounts are not external performance

Real MBG relationships: MBG account 89010 and Riverton account 89011 were reciprocal at $850,000.00. MBG note receivable 89012 and Riverton note payable 89013 were reciprocal at $12,000.00 before a later $400.00 drift. Separate entity managers need valid responsibility reports, while consolidated reporting eliminates internal balances and transactions.

Responsibility accounting assigns performance to managers based on resources and decisions they influence. Transfer pricing values goods, services, financing, or assets exchanged among related responsibility centers. A price can motivate behavior, allocate profit, support legal-entity accounting, and affect tax or regulatory outcomes; one method rarely optimizes every purpose.

Types of responsibility centers

  • Cost center: manager controls cost for a defined service or output. Evaluate cost, quality, service, and efficiency.
  • Revenue center: manager primarily controls revenue activity; cost and margin still require safeguards.
  • Profit center: manager influences revenue and cost. Evaluate controllable margin and strategic drivers.
  • Investment center: manager influences profit and assets/capital employed. Evaluate ROI, residual income, and long-term value.

Classify based on actual authority, not title. A project manager who cannot set contract price or financing terms should not be evaluated as though controlling full entity profit. Responsibility reports separate controllable and noncontrollable items while preserving total economics.

Controllability and goal congruence

The controllability principle says managers should be evaluated primarily on items they can influence within the evaluation horizon. It does not remove accountability for escalation, forecasting, or mitigation. A manager may not control material-market inflation but can control timely procurement strategy and estimate updates.

Goal congruence exists when local decisions support group objectives. A transfer price that maximizes one entity's reported margin can damage group profit by causing another entity to reject an internally efficient source. Performance measures should not reward shifting cost, delaying maintenance, overbilling, or hoarding cash.

Transfer-pricing methods

Market-based price uses an external comparable and supports autonomy when a competitive market exists. Adjust for freight, selling cost, quality, volume, and terms. Cost-based price may use variable cost, full cost, or cost plus markup. It is practical but can transfer inefficiency and create disputes over cost allocation. Negotiated price uses bargaining within a feasible range but depends on information and power. Dual pricing records different internal prices for buyer and seller with a central offset; it supports incentives but complicates reporting.

Tax rules for cross-border and related-party transactions require arm's-length support; this lesson does not invent tax conclusions. Legal agreements and entity accounting remain distinct from internal performance reports.

Opportunity cost and the transfer range

The minimum transfer price from the seller's perspective is:

Incremental cost per unit + opportunity cost per unit

The buyer's maximum is the cost of the best external alternative adjusted for relevant differences.

Assume an illustrative MBG service unit has variable cost $80 per hour and unused capacity. Riverton can buy externally for $120. With no opportunity cost, feasible transfer price lies between $80 and $120. Any price in the range benefits the group relative to external purchase, ignoring quality and transaction differences.

If the seller is at capacity and can earn $50 contribution margin from an external customer, minimum becomes $80 + $50 = $130. Because buyer's maximum remains $120, no mutually beneficial internal transfer exists; external purchase preserves greater group contribution.

Worked responsibility report

Assume an illustrative project profit center reports $2,000,000 revenue, $1,400,000 direct controllable cost, $200,000 allocated shared overhead, and $100,000 financing cost controlled centrally. Contribution before allocations is $600,000. Reported accounting profit after all allocations is $300,000.

For manager evaluation, show the $600,000 controllable contribution and relevant quality/schedule measures. Show $200,000 overhead allocation and $100,000 financing separately. This does not remove them from entity profit; it prevents evaluation from implying control the project manager lacks. If the manager influences shared-resource consumption, an activity-based charge may be partly controllable.

Real intercompany reconciliation before performance

For the $850,000.00 real reciprocal pair, confirm entity, exact accounts, sign, period, currency, counterparty, and source. For the $12,000.00 note pair, trace the later $400.00 drift rather than forcing elimination. MBG and MF are the source of truth for their intercompany numbers; subsidiaries conform after investigation.

Eliminate valid reciprocal balances in consolidation. Internal revenue and expense may also require elimination, along with unrealized profit in assets when applicable. Separate responsibility reports can retain transfer charges for performance, but consolidated statements cannot report the group selling to itself.

Trade AP account 211 does not eliminate merely because entities are related. Identify the actual counterparty. A third-party obligation remains a group liability.

Behavioral and ethical controls

Transfer prices can motivate dysfunctional behavior: sourcing a worse external option to improve one center's metrics, delaying transfers, shifting fixed cost, or manipulating capacity claims. Establish dispute resolution, comparable-data governance, periodic review, and reconciliation between managerial and legal-entity books.

Do not change internal pricing retroactively solely to hit bonus targets. Document method, rationale, effective date, approvals, and exceptions. Use multiple measures so short-term center profit does not dominate customer, quality, safety, cash, or strategic capacity.

Service-department costs and shared resources

Shared functions such as IT, payroll, procurement, or equipment support may be allocated using direct, step-down, or reciprocal methods. The direct method ignores services among support departments. Step-down recognizes some support in a chosen sequence. The reciprocal method recognizes mutual services and is conceptually most complete, though more complex.

Select drivers based on consumption: tickets, users, payroll checks, purchase orders, machine-hours, or square footage. Revenue is convenient but often weakly causal. Publish rates and actual usage so centers can understand charges. Separate capacity supplied from capacity used where decisions require it; charging unused central capacity to operating units can distort performance.

Transfer-price reconciliation

Maintain a bridge from internal management charges to legal-entity accounts and consolidated eliminations. Each transfer should retain seller, buyer, service/product, quantity, rate, amount, period, agreement, and reciprocal posting. Reconcile both count and dollars. Differences can arise from timing, exchange rates, markup, quantity disputes, or one-sided posting.

The fictionalized $400.00 note drift demonstrates why reciprocal validation cannot be annual. A transfer-pricing policy does not authorize plugging unmatched balances. Correct entity books based on source evidence, then eliminate valid reciprocals.

Evaluate decisions using relevant cost independent of the booked transfer price. A transfer price allocates reported profit but does not change consolidated cash paid to external parties. If one center's “cost” is another center's internal revenue, eliminate both when analyzing group contribution, while retaining genuine incremental external cost and opportunity cost.

Use capacity assumptions consistently. A seller with idle capacity has zero opportunity cost for the unused resource only if the transfer does not displace other work or create capacity-related cost. Expected future demand, quality, scheduling, and strategic capability may still matter.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR tests responsibility-center classification, controllable margin, ROI effects, opportunity-cost transfer pricing, and segment analysis. Always solve from the group's relevant economics first, then consider manager incentives and reporting layers.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify each center by real decision authority.
  2. Separate controllable results from allocated and central items.
  3. Calculate seller minimum and buyer maximum using opportunity cost.
  4. Reconcile legal-entity reciprocals before elimination.
  5. Bridge responsibility reports to entity and consolidated statements.
  6. Monitor behavioral consequences and approve method changes.

Recap: responsibility accounting assigns influence, not blame. Transfer pricing must support group economics, manager behavior, entity records, and compliance without mistaking $850,000.00 of internal reciprocity for external value creation.

weeks.title: ROI, Residual Income, EVA & Surety Performance (CMA P1-C · feeds P2-A/BAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — performance determines capacity

Real MBG context: a vehicle and equipment loan reconciliation covered 13 accounts and tied post-adjustment to $310,000.00. Sureties and lenders look beyond profit to working capital, leverage, backlog quality, cash, and reliable WIP estimates. A project can report margin while consuming liquidity; an entity can grow revenue while reducing bonding capacity.

Performance measures translate accounting data into decision signals. ROI, residual income, and economic value added evaluate returns relative to capital. Their usefulness depends on consistent definitions, correct entity boundaries, and adjustments for accounting choices.

Return on investment

ROI = Operating income ÷ Average operating assets

DuPont decomposition gives:

ROI = (Operating income ÷ Sales) × (Sales ÷ Average operating assets)

The first term is operating margin; the second is asset turnover. A manager can improve ROI through price/mix, cost control, asset utilization, working capital, or disposal of unproductive assets. Each action has risk: delaying necessary investment or rejecting good projects can increase current ROI while harming value.

Assume an illustrative division has $400,000 operating income, $4,000,000 sales, and $2,000,000 average operating assets. Margin is 10%, turnover 2.0, and ROI 20%. The decomposition ties: 10% × 2.0 = 20%.

Residual income

Residual income = Operating income − (Required rate × Average operating assets)

Using the illustrative division and a 12% required rate, capital charge is $240,000 and residual income is $160,000. Residual income encourages acceptance of projects earning above the required rate even if they reduce the division's percentage ROI.

Suppose a new illustrative project requires $500,000 and earns $80,000, a 16% return. It exceeds the 12% requirement and adds $20,000 residual income. Combined operating income becomes $480,000 and assets $2,500,000, so combined ROI falls from 20% to 19.2%. An ROI-only manager may reject a value-adding project; residual income aligns better with absolute value creation.

Residual income favors larger centers in absolute dollars, so compare trends and scale carefully. Required rates should reflect risk and capital policy rather than being changed to produce desired rankings.

Economic value added

EVA is a refined residual-income concept:

EVA = NOPAT − (WACC × Invested capital)

NOPAT is net operating profit after tax; invested capital is operating capital supplied by debt and equity; WACC is the weighted average cost of capital. EVA may adjust accounting measures to better approximate economic investment and performance, such as selected R&D, leases, or nonrecurring items, depending on the defined system.

Assume illustrative NOPAT of $500,000, invested capital $3,000,000, and WACC 10%. EVA is $200,000. Positive EVA means operating return exceeded the capital charge; it does not mean cash increased by $200,000.

Measurement choices

Define the numerator and denominator consistently. If operating income excludes interest, operating assets should exclude financing assets/liabilities as defined. Use average assets because income spans a period. Gross versus net book value changes ROI as assets age; net book value can make an unchanged operation appear to improve through depreciation alone.

Allocations and transfer prices affect segment income. Idle assets, construction WIP, goodwill, leases, and shared cash require policy. Do not compare MBG and Riverton using different definitions or combine their capital without a clear consolidated measure and eliminations.

Inflation, accounting estimates, and project timing can distort measures. Pair financial ratios with WIP quality, forecast accuracy, schedule, safety, customer, and control indicators.

Surety and bonding lens

Surety underwriting commonly considers character, capacity, and capital. Financial analysis may include working capital, net worth, leverage, profitability, cash flow, backlog, job schedule quality, under/overbillings, and loss history. Exact underwriting formulas and thresholds vary by surety; do not invent a universal “bonding capacity equals X times working capital” rule.

Basic measures include:

Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities

Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities

Debt-to-equity = Total debt ÷ Equity

Assume an illustrative entity has $3,000,000 current assets, $2,000,000 current liabilities, $1,500,000 debt, and $2,500,000 equity. Working capital is $1,000,000, current ratio 1.5, and debt-to-equity 0.6.

Classify assets realistically. Stale or unsupported WIP and uncollectible receivables weaken quality even when included in current assets. Overbilling may provide cash but represents future performance. Underbilling may be an asset but also signals financing of work or billing/collectibility risk.

Backlog and profit fade

Backlog is remaining contract value on awarded work under a defined policy. Gross backlog alone is not profit or cash. Analyze expected margin, duration, customer, geography, capacity, financing, and cancellation/change-order risk.

A backlog profit estimate should reconcile to job schedules. Gross-profit fade reduces expected future earnings and may signal weak estimating or execution. A surety values timely recognition of problems more than optimistic delay. The real discipline from MBG's exact-amount convention and WIP review supports credibility.

Real debt context and decisions

The fictionalized $310,000.00 post-adjustment vehicle/equipment loan total is a verified portfolio balance, not an illustrative WACC input. Performance analysis should tie debt schedules to the GL, separate principal and interest, confirm collateral and maturities, and model cash service. Equipment may improve capacity and margin but consumes capital and can reduce liquidity.

When evaluating an equipment investment, measure incremental NOPAT, working capital, maintenance, tax effects, disposal value, and capital employed. Do not evaluate only the accounting depreciation or the debt payment.

Measure design and gaming risk

ROI can rise when a manager delays maintenance, reduces training, accelerates revenue, or disposes assets needed for future growth. Residual income can encourage scale but may still reward short-horizon accounting income. EVA attempts economic adjustments but becomes opaque if adjustments are numerous or discretionary. Use transparent definitions and multi-year trends.

Investment decisions should use incremental cash flows and risk-adjusted discount rates; accounting performance measures evaluate stewardship after or during investment. Do not approve a project solely because its first-year ROI is high or reject it solely because depreciation lowers accounting income.

Use beginning, ending, or average assets consistently. Average operating assets usually aligns a period's income with capital employed, but major mid-period acquisitions may require monthly weighting. Decide treatment of construction in progress, idle equipment, leased assets, accumulated depreciation, and allocated corporate assets before comparing centers.

Surety package controls

A defensible surety package reconciles trial balance, WIP schedule, backlog, receivables, under/overbillings, debt schedules, cash, and covenant calculations. Explain significant fade, loss jobs, aged underbillings, stale receivables, and intercompany balances. Do not improve ratios by netting unrelated accounts or moving obligations across entities.

Stress test backlog. Assume illustratively $10,000,000 backlog at 15% expected gross margin, or $1,500,000 profit. If estimated cost rises enough to reduce margin to 10%, expected profit falls to $1,000,000—a $500,000 fade. Model the liquidity needed to perform the remaining work and the timing of billings, not profit alone.

Qualitative credibility matters. Timely, exact, reconciled reporting can support confidence; unexplained changes and repeated late loss recognition weaken it. The goal is not to present the most favorable ratio but to demonstrate controlled capacity to complete obligations.

CMA Part 2 / BAR Crossover

Part 2 expands ratio analysis, cost of capital, value creation, and financing. BAR connects performance measures to analytical conclusions and forecast assumptions. Expect questions where ROI and residual income recommend different decisions.

Practice and recap

  1. Define operating income and assets consistently.
  2. Decompose ROI into margin and turnover.
  3. Use residual income to test projects against required return.
  4. Calculate EVA from NOPAT and a capital charge.
  5. Evaluate surety ratios with asset quality and WIP evidence.
  6. Connect backlog, debt, cash, and operating capacity.

Recap: ROI measures rate, residual income measures dollars above a required return, and EVA measures operating profit after an economic capital charge. Surety analysis adds liquidity, leverage, backlog, and reporting credibility.

weeks.title: Balanced Scorecard & Entity Segment Reporting (CMA P1-C · feeds BAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — side by side, never silently combined

Real MBG control totals: MBG's GL was $12,480,000.00 and Riverton's $16,920,000.00; MBG WIP was $14,480,000.00 and Riverton WIP $11,360,000.00. Both entities can appear on one management dashboard, but their bank accounts, ledgers, risks, and legal obligations remain separate. A consolidated view requires explicit eliminations, not silent addition.

The balanced scorecard translates strategy into linked financial and nonfinancial objectives. Segment reporting evaluates meaningful business components. Together they prevent management from judging performance through a single short-term profit number.

Balanced scorecard perspectives

  1. Financial: profitability, cash, working capital, return, leverage, and surety capacity.
  2. Customer/stakeholder: satisfaction, repeat work, claims, quality, schedule, and owner relationships.
  3. Internal process: estimating, procurement, project execution, billing, close, safety, and control.
  4. Learning and growth: people, skills, systems, data, culture, and improvement capacity.

The perspectives form a strategy hypothesis. Training and data quality can improve estimating and project reviews; better processes can improve schedule and customer outcomes; those can improve margin and cash. Measures must test the logic rather than decorate a dashboard.

Design measures correctly

Each measure needs definition, purpose, owner, source, frequency, target, threshold, and action. Pair lagging outcomes with leading drivers. Gross margin is lagging; estimate-to-complete update timeliness is leading. Cash is lagging; billing package cycle time is a driver.

Balance quantity, quality, time, cost, and risk. A target for faster invoice processing can cause duplicate or misclassified payments unless quality controls remain. A target for maximum utilization can create burnout, safety risk, or deferred maintenance.

Avoid vanity metrics and denominator manipulation. “90% on time” requires a defined milestone population and rules for scope changes. Preserve historical definitions or clearly restate trends.

Worked scorecard

The following targets are illustrative:

PerspectiveMeasureTargetGuardrail
FinancialForecast gross marginAt least 18%No unresolved WIP reconciliation
CustomerMilestones on scheduleAt least 90%Approved scope baseline
ProcessCost-to-complete updates100% by day 3Operations and finance approval
Learning/controlKey reconciliations cross-trainedTwo trained ownersSegregated preparer/reviewer

Suppose illustratively 18 of 20 milestones are on time: 90%, target met. But two on-time milestones used unapproved scope reductions. The guardrail reveals that the headline percentage does not prove performance.

Segment and entity reporting

A management segment may be an entity, geography, service line, project type, or responsibility center. Define it based on how management allocates resources and assesses performance. External segment reporting follows applicable accounting guidance and may not match every internal view.

Build separate MBG and Riverton income statements, balance sheets, cash views, WIP schedules, and scorecards. Then present a group view with intercompany eliminations. The real reciprocal MBG 89010/Riverton 89011 balance of $850,000.00 is internal and eliminated in consolidation; trade AP 211 to third parties remains.

Do not compare dollar totals without scale and mix. Common-size statements, per-unit metrics, margin, turnover, and risk indicators can improve comparability. A developer with long-duration WIP should not be judged by the same short-cycle metrics as a service unit without adjustment.

Segment profit and allocations

Define segment margin layers:

  • Revenue less traceable variable/direct cost = contribution.
  • Less traceable fixed cost = segment margin.
  • Less allocated common cost = reported segment profit.

Common fixed costs that continue if a segment closes are not relevant to a keep/drop decision merely because allocated. Allocations remain necessary for full reporting and pricing in some contexts, but decision reports should distinguish traceable and allocated amounts.

Assume an illustrative segment has $1,500,000 revenue, $900,000 variable cost, $300,000 traceable fixed cost, and $200,000 allocated common cost. Contribution is $600,000, segment margin $300,000, and reported profit $100,000. Dropping it would not save the $200,000 common cost if that cost continues; group profit would fall $300,000 before other effects.

Entity-specific dashboard controls

Every dashboard row should retain entity, period, source, definition, and last refresh. Reconcile financial KPIs to exact ledgers and WIP schedules. Use role-based access so one entity's sensitive data is not improperly exposed. Preserve versions used in management decisions.

MBG uses bank 102.1 while Riverton uses 102. Group cash must identify restrictions and intercompany movements. Never use a consolidated total to authorize an entity payment without legal availability.

Use exception narratives with owner, cause, impact, action, and deadline. Red/amber/green status needs quantitative thresholds and cannot replace commentary for material items.

Behavior and incentives

Tying compensation to a single measure encourages gaming. Margin-only incentives can delay loss recognition; revenue targets can encourage poor contracts; cash targets can delay valid vendor payments; schedule targets can sacrifice quality. Use balanced measures, multi-period evaluation, clawbacks where appropriate, and independent data controls.

Targets must align with authority. Entity leaders can own controllable working capital and forecast quality; corporate treasury owns facility structure; finance owns definitions and reconciliation; operations owns project evidence. Shared accountability needs explicit decision rights.

Causal map and dashboard review

Build a causal chain explicitly. An illustrative initiative to cross-train project accountants should increase coverage of key reconciliations; that should reduce close delays and unresolved variances; faster reliable information should improve billing and cost decisions; those should improve cash and margin. Assign measures at each link. If training completion rises but reconciliation quality does not, investigate training design or staffing rather than assuming financial benefit.

Targets need baselines and time horizons. Improving on-time cost-to-complete updates from 70% to 95% over six months is different from declaring a permanent 100% target without capacity. Use control limits and trend where process variation matters. One red month may be noise; a sustained shift may require action.

Segment reconciliation

Create a bridge from segment results to entity totals and from entities to consolidated results. The bridge should show unallocated corporate items, intersegment transactions, eliminations, and accounting-policy differences. Segment revenue plus corporate/unallocated and elimination adjustments must equal consolidated revenue; the same discipline applies to profit and assets.

Assume illustratively MBG segment revenue $5,000,000, Riverton $4,000,000, and $600,000 internal revenue from MBG to Riverton. Summed entity revenue is $9,000,000, but consolidated external revenue is $8,400,000 after eliminating the internal $600,000. The elimination does not change each entity's legal ledger.

Review measure quality. Reconcile financial measures to controlled sources; validate nonfinancial populations; retain calculation versions; and test manual adjustments. Dashboard access should be appropriate, but transparency of definitions should not depend on privileged tribal knowledge.

During management review, focus on exceptions, cause, forecast impact, and action. Do not spend the meeting reading every green metric. Confirm that favorable results are complete and sustainable, especially when they conflict with cash, WIP, safety, or customer evidence.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR tests segment profitability, allocations, common-size analysis, scorecard causality, and management interpretation. Questions often ask whether a segment should be dropped or why a metric is misleading. Separate avoidable cost from allocated cost and entity performance from consolidated elimination.

Practice and recap

  1. Map strategy across four balanced-scorecard perspectives.
  2. Pair leading drivers with lagging outcomes and guardrails.
  3. Define segment margin layers and allocation policy.
  4. Prepare entity reports before consolidated views.
  5. Reconcile financial measures and govern nonfinancial sources.
  6. Review incentives for gaming and unintended risk.

Reliable definitions let leaders compare performance without rewarding accounting noise or hidden risk.

Recap: a balanced scorecard measures the system that creates results, while segment reporting shows where results arise. MBG and Riverton can share a dashboard without losing their separate identities or turning internal activity into external performance.

weeks.title: Job-Order Costing & Cost Codes to WIP GL (CMA P1-D · feeds FAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — one invoice, two ledgers

Real MBG structure: MBG carries $14,480,000.00 in account series 14xxxxx as work in progress. That total must be useful in two different ways. The general ledger must show controllable financial-statement categories, while the job-cost ledger must tell a project manager which job, phase, and activity consumed the money. Posting a framing invoice directly to a made-up GL account named after the cost code destroys that separation. The correct architecture is: detailed cost code for job tracking, mapped to a real WIP control account for the debit, with the vendor liability credited. MBG uses JCS as its job-cost GL; do not call it Ledgerline 100. MBG and Riverton also remain entity-segregated.

The salvaged mapping engine makes the rule explicit. Labor codes roll to 1401, materials to 1402, equipment to 1403, subcontractors to 1404, and other direct costs to 1405. Cost codes such as L004, M001, E001, S003, and O001 are dimensions, not GL accounts. A clean posting preserves both views without multiplying the chart of accounts.

Concept — job-order costing from first principles

Job-order costing accumulates costs for a distinct job, contract, or batch. It fits construction because each home or project has its own scope, estimate, change orders, and margin. A job-cost record normally captures the entity, job, cost code, cost type, amount, date, source document, and approver. The GL captures the financial account. The two records must reconcile: the sum of job detail mapped to a WIP control account must equal that control account's GL balance for the same entity and cutoff.

Three classifications matter. Direct costs can be traced economically to one job: jobsite lumber, crew time, a dedicated excavator rental, or a framing subcontract. Indirect production costs support multiple jobs and require a rational allocation, such as shared supervision or equipment depreciation. Period costs support the company rather than production and are expensed when incurred, such as general corporate administration. Classification determines whether a cost enters WIP, is allocated to jobs, or hits current expense.

The source document starts the control trail. A purchase order establishes authorization; receiving evidence establishes occurrence; the vendor invoice establishes the amount; job and cost-code approval establish classification. Payroll follows a parallel trail through approved time, PayStream ACH or MBG check, and job allocation. There is no cash labor. The posting engine should reject an invalid cost code and should never accept a cost code as the GL account.

The five-account rollup

Job-cost categoryIllustrative codeMapped WIP GL
LaborL004 Rough carpenter1401 WIP — Labor
MaterialsM001 Framing lumber1402 WIP — Materials
EquipmentE001 Excavator rental1403 WIP — Equipment
SubcontractorS003 Framing1404 WIP — Subcontractors
Other directO001 Permits and fees1405 WIP — Other direct costs

These account numbers and mappings are real app mapping rules. The sample transaction amounts below are illustrative because the source materials provide MBG's total WIP but not invoice-level amounts for these five codes.

Worked example — post, roll up, and reconcile

Assume an illustrative MBG framing package for Job H-101 contains $8,400 of framing lumber coded M001, $3,200 of rough-carpenter labor coded L004, and a $12,500 framing subcontract coded S003. Each line keeps Job H-101 and its cost code. The financial postings are:

AccountDebitCredit
1402 WIP — Materials$8,400—
1401 WIP — Labor$3,200—
1404 WIP — Subcontractors$12,500—
Cash/AP/payroll liabilities, as applicable—$24,100

The job-cost subsidiary record totals $24,100 for H-101. The WIP control-account additions also total $24,100. That equality is the first reconciliation. It does not prove cutoff, existence, or entity accuracy, so the accountant also traces each line to its source and confirms it belongs to MBG rather than Riverton.

Now add an illustrative $1,900 excavator rental coded E001 and a $600 permit coded O001. The job total becomes $26,600, while the control-account rollup becomes: 1401 $3,200; 1402 $8,400; 1403 $1,900; 1404 $12,500; 1405 $600. Their sum is $26,600. If JCS shows $26,600 in job detail but only $24,700 in the mapped GL additions, the $1,900 variance points directly to the equipment line. A total-only comparison would show that something is wrong; category rollup shows where to investigate.

At period end, use a rollforward for each WIP control account: beginning WIP plus additions plus or minus reclasses minus transfers to cost of sales equals ending WIP. Keep job reclasses separate from external additions. Moving a cost from one job to another within the same WIP GL account changes subsidiary detail but has zero GL impact. Moving a cost between cost categories changes the WIP control accounts but not total WIP. When a completed home closes, the relevant accumulated cost transfers from WIP to cost of sales; it does not remain an asset indefinitely.

Predetermined overhead rate

Job-order systems often apply overhead using a predetermined rate: estimated production overhead divided by estimated allocation-base activity. If illustrative annual production overhead is $480,000 and expected direct-labor hours are 24,000, the rate is $20 per direct-labor hour. A job using 160 hours receives $3,200 of applied overhead. Actual overhead and applied overhead are compared at period end. Underapplied overhead means actual overhead exceeded applied overhead; overapplied means applied exceeded actual. The allocation base must have a causal or beneficial relationship to the cost pool.

Why the controls matter

A cost code should be granular enough to support estimating and accountability but stable enough to compare jobs. Creating a new code for every invoice makes trends meaningless. Using one broad code hides overruns. The chart of accounts should remain even more stable: it answers financial-reporting questions, while dimensions answer operational questions. This separation is a core design principle in accounting information systems.

Reconciliation must use exact account numbers and a consistent cutoff. The Master Brain warns that JCS's “Acct Ending Bal” is not cumulative; calculate true ending balance from beginning balance plus year-to-date debits minus year-to-date credits. Also avoid substring searches: searching “1401” can capture unintended job-cost strings. Tie exact mapped detail to the exact GL account, then tie the combined 14xxxxx WIP balance to the trial balance. The real MBG total of $14,480,000.00 is the anchor, not a substitute for job-level proof.

CPA Crossover — FAR

FAR asks whether costs qualify for capitalization and how assets and expenses are classified. The CMA emphasis is cost accumulation and managerial use; FAR adds recognition and presentation. For MBG, valid construction costs accumulate as a WIP/CIP asset while the related performance remains in process, subject to the applicable contract and inventory guidance. General inefficiency, abnormal waste, and unrelated administrative costs do not become assets merely because management assigns a job code. A dimension cannot override recognition rules.

Practice — perform the close test

  1. Select one entity and cutoff; never combine MBG and Riverton.
  2. Export exact-account GL activity for 1401–1405 and job-cost detail from JCS.
  3. Map every valid cost code to one WIP control account and quarantine invalid codes.
  4. Reconcile by job, control account, and total; explain every variance to $0.00.
  5. Trace samples to invoice, payroll, approval, and job evidence.
  6. Separate additions, job reclasses, category reclasses, and closeout transfers.
  7. Review stale WIP and completed jobs that should have transferred to cost of sales.

Recap: job-order costing answers “what did this job consume?” The GL answers “what financial resource or obligation changed?” Cost codes preserve detail; WIP control accounts preserve financial-statement integrity. A valid system posts both views, reconciles them exactly, and maintains entity and period boundaries.

weeks.title: WIP Schedule & Over/Under Billings (CMA P1-D · feeds FAR/BAR)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the schedule behind $14 million

Real balances: MBG carries $14,480,000.00 in the 14xxxxx WIP account series, and Riverton carries $11,360,000.00. Those balances belong to different entities and must never be combined. They are not cash, billings, or current-period expense. They are accumulated job costs recorded as a balance-sheet asset while the related projects remain in process. A WIP schedule must explain which jobs comprise the total, how much performance has been earned, what has been billed, and whether each estimate is still credible.

The danger is not merely arithmetic. A late vendor invoice understates cost to date. An optimistic estimate to complete overstates percentage complete and gross profit. A reversal posted to the wrong job can manufacture a margin swing. A project can appear profitable while consuming cash because earned revenue exceeds billings. The WIP schedule joins the job-cost system, contract data, billing records, and the GL so those contradictions become visible.

Concept — five columns that drive the answer

For a performance obligation satisfied over time, ASC 606 permits an input method when that method faithfully depicts performance. In construction, cost-to-cost is common:

Percentage complete = eligible costs incurred to date ÷ current estimated total eligible cost

Revenue recognized to date = transaction price × percentage complete

Gross profit recognized to date = revenue recognized to date − cost recognized to date

Contract position = revenue recognized to date − billings to date

A positive contract position means earned revenue exceeds billings: an underbilling presented as a contract asset, subject to the specific contract facts. A negative position means billings exceed earned revenue: an overbilling presented as a contract liability. Billings are not revenue by themselves. Cash collections are not revenue by themselves. Performance drives recognition; billing and collection drive receivables and cash.

The denominator is a forecast, not a historical fact. Estimated total cost equals cost to date plus the latest estimate to complete. It must incorporate approved scope, remaining quantities, committed subcontracts, labor productivity, procurement risk, and known rework. Costs that do not depict performance—such as certain significant uninstalled materials or abnormal waste—may require adjustment rather than mechanically accelerating progress.

Required schedule fields

  • Entity, job, project manager, and cutoff date.
  • Original contract plus approved modifications forming the current transaction price.
  • Original and current estimated total cost.
  • Cost to date, estimate to complete, and percentage complete.
  • Revenue and gross profit recognized to date and in the current period.
  • Billings to date and the resulting contract asset or liability.
  • Prior-period margin and current margin to expose fade or gain.
  • Reconciliation from the job schedule to exact WIP GL balances.

Worked example — a 75% job

Use the following illustrative amounts; the structure is real, but these amounts are not asserted to be an MBG job:

LineCalculationAmount
Contract priceGiven$2,000,000
Estimated total costGiven$1,600,000
Estimated total gross profit$2,000,000 − $1,600,000$400,000
Cost to dateGiven$1,200,000
Percentage complete$1,200,000 ÷ $1,600,00075%
Revenue to date75% × $2,000,000$1,500,000
Gross profit to date$1,500,000 − $1,200,000$300,000
Billings to dateGiven$1,400,000
Contract asset$1,500,000 − $1,400,000$100,000 underbilled

Three independent checks agree. First, 75% of the $400,000 estimated gross profit is $300,000. Second, revenue of $1,500,000 less cost of $1,200,000 is $300,000. Third, earned revenue of $1,500,000 less billings of $1,400,000 is a $100,000 contract asset. The job has performed more than it has billed, so MBG is financing that timing gap until it submits and collects the next billing.

Assume illustratively that prior-period revenue and gross profit were $1,260,000 and $252,000. Current-period revenue is $240,000 and current-period gross profit is $48,000. A cumulative schedule must subtract prior recognized amounts; recording the entire to-date amount again would double count revenue and profit.

Estimate changes, fade, and loss contracts

Now suppose remaining cost is reassessed and current estimated total cost rises from $1,600,000 to an illustrative $1,800,000, while contract price remains $2,000,000. At $1,200,000 cost to date, revised progress is 66.67%. Revised revenue to date is about $1,333,333 and revised gross profit to date is about $133,333. Compared with the original $300,000 cumulative profit, the estimate change creates a $166,667 cumulative catch-up reduction. It does not rewrite issued prior statements; the current estimate changes the cumulative amount required now.

Gross-profit fade is the decline in estimated margin from one reporting date to the next. Here estimated total profit falls from $400,000 to $200,000 and margin falls from 20% to 10%. Fade can signal missed costs, weak productivity, unapproved change orders, purchasing pressure, or premature prior estimates. Gain is the opposite, but unexpected gains also deserve challenge because they may reflect omitted commitments or cutoff errors.

If the current estimate indicates an overall contract loss, recognize the expected loss in full when required by the applicable loss guidance; do not spread it across the remaining percentage. For example, an illustrative $2,000,000 contract with estimated total cost of $2,080,000 has an $80,000 total expected loss. The fact that the job is only partly complete does not justify reporting only a fraction of the expected loss.

From schedule to entries and proof

A conceptual current-period entry records construction expense and revenue for the period and establishes the net contract position as needed by the entity's system design. Billing entries separately debit accounts receivable and credit billings or the contract-position account. Collection separately debits cash and credits receivables. System account names vary, but the schedule must prevent billing activity from becoming a substitute for earned revenue.

For close, freeze a cutoff and reconcile four directions. Costs to date tie by job to JCS and by exact account to the 14xxxxx GL. Contract price ties to executed contracts and approved modifications. Billings tie to the billing subledger. Prior recognized revenue and profit tie to the prior close. Then perform analytical review: jobs over 100% complete, negative estimates to complete, margins outside expectations, large underbillings, stale costs, completed jobs with WIP, and unexplained post-acquisition reversals all require resolution. The real MBG $14,480,000.00 balance is not proven merely because a spreadsheet total happens to match; job composition and cutoff must also be valid.

The JCS warning still applies: “Acct Ending Bal” is not cumulative. Derive true balance from beginning plus year-to-date debits minus year-to-date credits. Exact account matching also matters because substring selection can capture unrelated data. Bank ties beat GL for cash, but WIP proof is anchored to supported job detail and the trial balance.

CPA Crossover — FAR and BAR

FAR tests ASC 606's five-step model, over-time criteria, input methods, contract assets, contract liabilities, and estimate changes. BAR emphasizes analysis: why margin moved, whether forecasts are biased, and how underbilling affects liquidity. An underbilling may increase reported current assets while worsening cash flow; an overbilling may support cash while creating a performance obligation. The labels are not value judgments. They are timing positions that must be understood alongside margin and cash.

Practice and recap

  1. Recompute percentage complete from current eligible costs and current estimated total cost.
  2. Recompute cumulative revenue and profit, then subtract prior recognition for current-period amounts.
  3. Compare earned revenue with billings and classify each job's contract position.
  4. Reconcile schedule costs to exact-account JCS detail and the entity's GL.
  5. Challenge fade, gain, unapproved changes, stale WIP, and reversals.
  6. Document whether every amount is real and sourced or illustrative.

Recap: the WIP schedule converts cost records and forecasts into revenue, profit, and contract position. Cost-to-cost is only as reliable as its numerator, denominator, and cutoff. Keep MBG and Riverton separate, keep billings distinct from earnings, and make every cumulative amount tie forward from the prior close.

weeks.title: Job-Cost Reclass & Gross vs Net Footing (CMA P1-D)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — why $31,250.00 becomes $32,650.00

Real MBG reclass: Q2-only cost must move from job CD 26 Q1 to CD 26 Q2. The net economic cost moved is $31,250.00, yet each side of the balanced journal entry foots to $32,650.00. The difference is not a typo. Account 25056 contains a fictionalized $700 credit that moves opposite the debit-balance cost lines. Because that credit reduces net cost by $700 but contributes $700 to the other side of the entry, the debit/credit footing exceeds the net moved amount by $1,400.

This is a classic exam and close trap: “amount moved,” “gross activity,” and “balanced JE footing” answer different questions. A preparer who forces the footing to equal the net cost can reverse the credit incorrectly or omit it. A reviewer who looks only at a zero net GL impact can miss that the wrong jobs or periods were used.

Concept — reclassification is correction of dimensions

A job-cost reclass changes where an already-recorded cost is attributed. It is not a new purchase, payment, or expense. When the original and destination use the same GL account, the entry debits and credits that same GL account with different job dimensions. Total GL balance is unchanged, while each job's subsidiary balance changes. The source job is relieved and the destination job is charged for debit-balance costs.

Period cutoff determines how much moves. The real MBG method is June year-to-date through period 6 minus March year-to-date through period 3, account by account. This isolates the Q2 increment and leaves $7,125.00 of fictionalized Jan–Mar Q1 cost in CD 26 Q1. Using June YTD alone would incorrectly move both Q1 and Q2. Using transaction dates without checking posting period could miss late-posted or backdated activity. The defensible population is derived from consistent cumulative balances and then traced to detailed activity.

Four amounts reviewers must distinguish

  • Signed line amount: debit-balance cost is positive; a credit balance offsets it.
  • Net cost moved: algebraic sum of signed source balances, here fictionalized $31,250.00.
  • Absolute gross activity: sum of absolute values, here fictionalized $32,650.00.
  • JE footing: total debits and total credits in the balanced reclass, also $32,650.00 per side.

With one $700 credit, let positive debit balances total D. Then D − $700 = $31,250.00, so D = $31,950.00. Absolute gross activity is $31,950.00 + $700 = $32,650.00. The spread between gross and net is $1,400, exactly twice the absolute credit. This relationship is a powerful control: gross − net = 2 × absolute value of opposite-sign items when all other lines share one sign.

Worked example — construct the balanced entry

The following aggregation uses the fictionalized case totals but illustrative grouping because the source excerpt does not provide every account-level line. Suppose debit-balance Q2 increments across several 14xxxxx cost accounts total $31,950.00, and account 25056 has a $700 credit increment. Signed net cost is $31,250.00.

For the debit-balance cost lines, relieve the wrong job and charge the right job:

GL account/dimensionDebitCredit
14xxxxx — Job CD 26 Q2$31,950.00—
14xxxxx — Job CD 26 Q1—$31,950.00

The $700 credit-balance line moves in the opposite direction. To remove a credit from CD 26 Q1, debit that source dimension; to establish it in CD 26 Q2, credit the destination:

GL account/dimensionDebitCredit
25056 — Job CD 26 Q1$700.00—
25056 — Job CD 26 Q2—$700.00

Total debits are $32,650.00 and total credits are $32,650.00. The source job's signed net cost falls by $31,250.00, and the destination job's signed net cost rises by $31,250.00. Each GL account nets to zero because its debit and credit use different job dimensions but the same account. Total company assets, liabilities, and profit do not change solely from the job reclass.

The open source issue must remain visible: the Master Brain says a possible “second $700” in account 25056 is awaiting Ken's pointer, while the trial balance shows only one $700 posted in May and carried to June. Do not invent or duplicate the second amount. The correct current lesson and JE use the proven one-$700 population and label the unresolved item for follow-up.

Build the workpaper so it can be audited

Start with an objective: move only Q2 increments, preserve Q1 cost, and maintain zero net by GL account. Include columns for entity, GL account, account description, source job, destination job, March YTD, June YTD, calculated increment, sign, absolute amount, source posting, destination posting, and supporting detail reference. Protect formulas and make totals visible.

Use these controls:

  1. Population: June YTD minus March YTD by exact account; do not use substring matches.
  2. Cutoff: investigate transactions whose document date and posting period disagree.
  3. Completeness: reconcile calculated increments to detailed Q2 activity, accounting for valid late postings.
  4. Account preservation: every source GL account must equal its destination GL account unless a separately approved account reclass is intended.
  5. Dimension reversal: source and destination jobs must be opposite on each paired line.
  6. Balance: total debits equal total credits at $32,650.00.
  7. Net transfer: destination signed net change equals $31,250.00 and source equals negative $31,250.00.
  8. After-post proof: rerun both jobs and exact accounts; Q1 keeps $7,125.00 of Jan–Mar cost.

Zero GL impact is necessary but not sufficient. An entry can balance while using the wrong jobs, duplicating a line, reversing the wrong period, or moving an unsupported amount. The reconciliation must prove both financial-account neutrality and correct job attribution.

Error patterns and their signatures

If the entry feet to $31,250.00 per side, the $700 opposite-sign line was probably netted away rather than posted. If the entry feet to $33,350.00, a second $700 may have been added without support. If Q1 ending cost goes to zero, the preparer likely moved June YTD instead of the Q2 increment. If total GL changes, the source and destination accounts do not match or one side is missing. If job changes equal $32,650.00 net, absolute values were summed as though all costs shared one sign.

Reclasses can also affect management reporting even when financial statements do not change. Job margin, project-manager performance, estimate-to-complete analysis, and WIP exception reports depend on correct dimensions. That is why the entry requires operational approval and why the destination job cannot be guessed from a description.

Exam connection

CMA questions test cost assignment, relevant classifications, responsibility reporting, and internal controls over adjustments. The underlying lesson is algebraic discipline: preserve signs, distinguish net change from gross flow, and understand which cost object changes. This week has no separate CPA crossover in the blueprint, but the audit trail and cutoff reasoning support FAR and AUD practice.

Practice and recap

Reperform the proof without looking at the answer: debit-balance increments of $31,950.00 plus a $700 credit produce net cost of $31,250.00, gross activity of $32,650.00, and balanced JE footing of $32,650.00 per side. Then explain why the credit is debited on the source job and credited on the destination job.

Reviewer discipline matters because dimensional errors can survive an otherwise balanced trial balance and distort management decisions for months.

Recap: a job reclass corrects a cost object, not total company cost. Use period-to-period YTD differences, preserve GL accounts, respect signs, and validate both the $31,250.00 net transfer and the $32,650.00 footing. The $1,400 spread is proof of the one $700 opposite-sign line, not an unexplained variance.

weeks.title: Overhead Allocation, ABC, Supply Chain & Retainage (CMA P1-D · feeds REG)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — labor cost is more than gross pay

Real MBG environment: payroll flows through PayStream and Apex Staffing, and labor must never be described or coded as cash labor. A job that receives only an employee's gross wage but none of the related employer taxes, insurance, supervision, or shared production support appears cheaper than it really is. That distorts job margin, bid pricing, WIP forecasts, and project-manager decisions.

At the same time, indiscriminately spreading every corporate cost across jobs is not better. Allocation is not a license to hide period expenses in WIP. The goal is to assign production overhead using drivers that reflect resource consumption, separate value-adding from non-value-adding activity, and preserve an audit trail from payroll or vendor source through the pool, rate, job, and GL. Retainage adds a second timing layer: MBG account 2120 is the real retention/retainage payable for holdbacks owed to subcontractors. A withheld payment does not reduce the job's incurred cost.

Concept — build a defensible allocation system

Direct labor and direct materials are traced when the cost-benefit relationship is clear. Indirect production costs are accumulated in homogeneous cost pools and allocated. A cost pool groups costs driven by similar activity. A cost driver measures consumption of that activity. The allocation rate equals estimated pool cost divided by expected driver volume; applied cost equals the rate multiplied by the job's actual driver units.

A traditional system may use one plantwide or department rate, such as direct-labor hours. That is simple and can be reasonable when jobs consume overhead similarly. Activity-based costing (ABC) uses multiple pools and drivers to reflect diversity. Procurement cost might follow purchase orders, setup cost might follow mobilizations, inspection cost might follow inspections, and equipment support might follow machine-hours. ABC improves visibility when low-volume complex jobs consume far more support than high-volume routine jobs.

More precision is not automatically better. A driver should be causal or beneficial, measurable, understandable, and worth maintaining. A pool that costs more to measure than it changes decisions creates false sophistication. Rates should be prospective and based on normal capacity where appropriate; allocating idle capacity or abnormal waste to active jobs can conceal operational problems.

Labor burden components

  • Employer payroll taxes and required contributions.
  • Workers' compensation and job-related insurance.
  • Production benefits and paid nonproductive time, when policy supports allocation.
  • Shared field supervision, safety, and payroll processing attributable to production.
  • Staffing-provider charges from Apex when they represent production labor or burden.

Each component needs a policy. Gross pay belongs to the employee and job supported by approved time. Employer obligations and production support may be traced or allocated. Employee withholdings are liabilities deducted from gross pay, not additional employer burden. Corporate finance, owner, or general administrative costs remain period costs unless authoritative recognition criteria and a defensible production relationship support different treatment.

Worked example — traditional burden versus ABC

All amounts in this worked example are illustrative. Suppose MBG estimates $360,000 of production overhead and 18,000 direct-labor hours for the year. A single traditional rate is $20 per direct-labor hour. Job A uses 600 hours and receives $12,000; Job B uses 200 hours and receives $4,000.

Now analysis shows two distinct pools: $180,000 of field support driven by 18,000 labor-hours, or $10 per hour, and $180,000 of procurement/inspection support driven by 900 activity events, or $200 per event. Job A uses 600 hours and 8 events, so ABC assigns $6,000 + $1,600 = $7,600. Job B uses 200 hours and 30 events, so ABC assigns $2,000 + $6,000 = $8,000.

JobTraditionalABCInterpretation
A$12,000$7,600High labor volume but low complexity
B$4,000$8,000Low labor volume but high support demand

The traditional system overcosts Job A by $4,400 and undercosts Job B by $4,000 relative to this ABC model. The remaining $400 reflects that the two sample jobs do not consume the entire period's driver capacity; it is not an arithmetic error to force into them. ABC changes product or job cost, not total company cost. Its decision value is exposing cross-subsidization.

Payroll posting

Assume illustrative approved PayStream payroll includes $10,000 gross direct labor for a job, $2,100 employee withholdings, $7,900 net pay by ACH, and $1,200 employer payroll taxes. If policy treats employer taxes as job burden, the job receives $11,200 of labor and burden, not merely the $7,900 cash disbursement and not $12,100. Employee withholdings are part of gross pay already; adding them again double counts labor. A conceptual posting debits WIP/direct labor $10,000 and WIP/applied burden $1,200, credits employee withholding liabilities $2,100, cash/payroll clearing $7,900, and employer tax liabilities $1,200.

Reconcile approved time to payroll, payroll to ACH or MBG check, liability accounts to filings, and job allocations to WIP. For Apex Staffing, trace the invoice and underlying worker/job support; do not assume every staffing charge has the same driver or entity.

Retainage 2120 — cost and cash occur at different times

Retainage is a contractual holdback intended to support completion and correction obligations. For MBG, account 2120 is the real retainage payable. Suppose an illustrative subcontractor earns $100,000 and the contract withholds 10%. MBG has incurred the full $100,000 job cost even though only $90,000 is currently payable in cash:

AccountDebitCredit
WIP — Subcontractor cost$100,000—
AP currently due—$90,000
2120 Retainage payable—$10,000

When contractual release conditions are met, reclassify or pay the $10,000 according to the AP workflow. The release does not create a second $10,000 of job cost. A common error is recording only the $90,000 current payment in WIP, understating cost to date and potentially overstating percentage complete margin. Another is treating retainage as a discount, even though the obligation remains.

Retainage also affects supply-chain behavior. Subcontractors finance the holdback and may reflect that cost in pricing. Long or disputed releases can weaken vendor liquidity, reduce competition, and increase lien or performance risk. A useful retainage aging report includes entity, vendor, job, original invoice, withheld amount, contract rate, substantial-completion status, release conditions, due date, approvals, and disputes. Reconcile its total to exact account 2120.

Supply chain and process improvement

Total cost of ownership extends beyond purchase price. A cheaper supplier can create more inspections, rework, expediting, downtime, warranty claims, and schedule delay. ABC makes these support costs visible. Supplier evaluation should combine price, quality, delivery reliability, lead-time variability, change-order behavior, compliance, capacity, and financial stability.

Process improvement starts with a flow: requisition, approved purchase order, receipt or field confirmation, invoice match, job/cost-code approval, retainage calculation, payment, and release. Remove duplicate entry, establish tolerances, and route exceptions rather than bypassing approval. A three-way match supports quantity, price, and occurrence, while job approval supports classification. Metrics can include first-pass match rate, purchase-order cycle time, rework cost, on-time delivery, invoice exceptions, retainage aging, and supplier defect rate.

Lean analysis distinguishes value-added work from non-value-added activity. Inspection may be necessary but is not the customer's desired output; prevention and process capability are usually better than repeated detection. Rework, waiting, excess movement, and duplicate approvals consume capacity. However, removing a control merely because it takes time is not improvement if it raises fraud, cutoff, or classification risk.

CPA Crossover — REG

REG intersects with payroll taxes, worker classification, and compliance. The accounting system must distinguish employee withholdings from employer taxes and retain support for payments and filings. The lesson is not to infer tax treatment from a cost-code label. A worker's legal classification and the entity's obligations depend on the actual facts and law. In MBG's convention, labor is paid through PayStream ACH or MBG check—never cash labor.

Practice and recap

  1. List production overhead pools and exclude unsupported corporate period costs.
  2. Select a measurable driver with a causal or beneficial relationship for each pool.
  3. Calculate prospective rates and identify unused or idle capacity separately.
  4. Reconcile PayStream/Apex source amounts through liabilities, payment, and job allocation.
  5. Record full subcontract cost while splitting current AP and real account 2120 retainage.
  6. Use ABC and supplier metrics to target rework and complexity, not merely spread cost.

Recap: tracing is preferred when practical; allocation is disciplined estimation when tracing is not. ABC reveals activity consumption, payroll burden completes labor cost, and retainage separates incurred cost from payment timing. Every method must preserve entity boundaries, source evidence, and exact reconciliation.
